1.pericope_label: Thou shalt not take thee a wife, neither shalt thou have sons or daughters in this place
debates: Whether the prophet was in fact unmarried
What kind of death is threatened
outliers: Calvin holds it does not matter whether the prophet was married, since the command came in a vision, but thinks it probable he was not, the celibacy being a living representation like the yoke and the walking naked
Calvin warns expressly that celibacy is not commended in this passage, as some have imagined from it
Gill and Calvin agree the deaths threatened are lingering rather than sudden, a continual languor worse to bear than being snatched away at once
Ellicott dates the message near the close of a reign in which the king trusted an Egyptian alliance, while Gill takes it as a continuation of what precedes
themes: A land judged unworthy of the blessing given to the whole race
A Latin poet quoted on rites of sepulture abandoned in a plague
Sudden death called happy by an ancient commander
A prophet forbidden marriage, mourning and mirth together

5.pericope_label: For thus saith the Lord, Enter not into the house of mourning, neither go to lament nor bemoan them: for I have taken away my peace from this people
debates: Whether the disputed verb means tear themselves or break bread
What the house of mourning was
Whether the cuttings and baldness are approved by being mentioned
outliers: Ellicott holds the marginal break bread for them gives the true meaning; Calvin argues the same from three ancient versions and two manuscripts, and from the correspondence of bread and drink in the two halves
Ellicott and Gill agree the word means a mourning-feast rather than a house of grief, the root meaning a shout applicable to joy or sorrow alike
Calvin insists the prophet does not mention the cuttings by way of commendation, since the law had forbidden imitating such customs
Ellicott takes the word peace in its highest power, as including all other blessings, once given and now withheld
themes: Cuttings believed to ease the dead and appease angry deities
A funeral feast suggested as the background of the Last Supper
The phrase rendered literally as the house of shouting
Men dying too fast to have leisure for mourning

10.pericope_label: Therefore will I cast you out of this land into a land that ye know not, neither ye nor your fathers; and there shall ye serve other gods day and night
debates: Whether the question is penitent or defiant
Whether serving other gods means compelled idolatry or only subjection to idolaters
How the eleventh and twelfth verses should be divided
outliers: Henry allows a penitent reading of the question but prefers the defiant one, of men who stand on their own justification and insinuate that they were wronged
Calvin rejects as too remote the milder reading that only subjection to idolaters is meant, and holds they were probably forced into ungodly ceremonies by conquerors who made sport of them
Calvin thinks the verses wrongly divided, and that joining the latter part of the eleventh to the twelfth removes the apparent repetition
Ellicott hears bitter irony in the sentence, that those who chose foreign gods at home shall serve them abroad in another sense
themes: The Jonah that raises the storm, offered to be thrown overboard
Conscience called a thousand witnesses
Conquerors compelling worship by way of daily sport
A single word corrected from imagination to stubbornness

14.pericope_label: Therefore, behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that it shall no more be said, The Lord liveth, that brought up the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt
debates: Whether the passage is consolation or an amplified threat
Why the later deliverance is called the greater
outliers: Calvin argues against the common exposition that a comfort is interposed for the faithful alone, and takes the passage as mixed, chiefly amplifying the threat by comparison with the servitude in Egypt
Gill reports three renderings of the opening word, therefore, notwithstanding, and surely, one authority taking it as an oath
Calvin holds the later redemption the greater miracle because less hope will remain, the name of Israel being extinguished and the temple destroyed
Gill grounds the same conclusion instead on the hardships of Babylon and the freshness of the later favour
themes: A land inferred to be higher than all others from a single verb
A people scattered like a body torn asunder
A redemption said to be remembered to the end of the world
Mercy and judgment so interwoven that neither can be separated

16.pericope_label: Behold, I will send for many fishers, saith the Lord, and they shall fish them; and after will I send for many hunters, and they shall hunt them
debates: Who the fishers and hunters are
What the carcasses of their detestable things are
outliers: Gill lists five candidates for the fishers, the Egyptians, the Chaldeans, the Medes and Persians, a later leader recalling the captives, and the apostles, and prefers the Chaldeans
Ellicott calls the application to the preachers of the gospel an after-thought whose source is a later saying, and Calvin calls it wholly foreign to the subject
Ellicott gives double a legal sense, restitution at twice the wrong being the normal standard under the law, while Gill and Wesley deny it means twice what the sins deserved
Calvin renders the word first as from the beginning and reads God gathering the buried iniquities of fathers and children into one bundle
themes: A great army described as drag-netting whole islands
Doctrine called a seasoning added to prophecy
Refuge taken in caves and driven out again
Idols called lifeless carcasses

19.pericope_label: Shall a man make gods unto himself, and they are no gods?
debates: What the argument about making gods amounts to
Whether the last verse looks to the captivity, the restoration, or both
Why the prophet turns abruptly to prayer
outliers: Calvin rejects as frigid the reading that the point is only that images cannot change their nature, and takes the argument to be that the created cannot be the creator
Calvin holds the therefore of the last verse infers from both captivity and restoration, the restoration being as remarkable an interposition as the captivity if not more so
Calvin explains the turn to prayer as a defence against the thought that the covenant with Abraham had been made void
Gill alone reads the last verse forward, of the Gentiles being made to know the true God through the gospel
themes: Satan called an acute disputant and a sophist
A man called an ephemeral animal whose life is like a shadow
A gracious promise called a light amid much darkness
Israel abasing herself below the level of those turning to her God
